newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish credit growth slowdown seen as bond-positive.
newsitem.headline: Irish credit growth slowdown seen as bond-positive.

text.p: An unexpected fall in the growth rate of Irish private sector credit in September should prove positive for Irish bonds and help ease recent tension in the interbank market, analysts said.

Figures released on Thursday showed that underlying private sector credit growth eased to 13.3 percent in September from a revised 14.2 percent in August. Analysts' forecasts for credit growth had ranged from 14.1 percent to 14.8 percent.
"The fall in the headline number to 13.3 percent is very positive for the market," said Padhraic Garvey, economist at Riada Stockbrokers.
Garvey said there had been some fairly severe curve flattening in Irish bonds in recent days, partly in anticipation of the credit data.

"We should see the curve steepen back up again over the next day or so. There were fears that a strong number would push up interbank rates and cause a panic at the short end but those fears have been overdone and the short end should outperform on the back of these numbers," he said.
Dealers said the short-dated bonds had already shown a positive reaction to the data, edging back into positive territory after losing ground earlier in the day.
By 1743 GMT, the eight percent bond due 2006 stood at 105.95 to yield 6.16 percent, up 30 pence from 105.65 before the data.
But analysts warned there was a danger that the market reaction could be overdone.

"We've seen the Exchequer returns for October and tax receipts were very strong so I would be surprised if the fall that we've seen in credit growth is sustained next month," said Goodbody Stockbrokers chief economist Han de Jong.
He noted the central bank pointed out in a statement accompanying the data that credit growth remained high and had increased by 7.5 percent in the six months to end-September.
"They are perhaps dampening euphoric ideas about these lower figures," de Jong said.
Alan McQauid, economist at Bloxham Stockbrokers, also believes credit growth could rise again in October.

"Despite the fall in the demand for money in September, these latest banking figures will provide little comfort for the Central Bank, as the bottom line is that underlying credit growth and residential mortgage lending remain too high for comfort."
But Riada's Garvey expects credit growth to level off over the balance of this year before slowing down in 1997.

"The economy is obviously still growing quite strongly but there is evidence that retail sales are levelling off, that the manufacturing side has slown down and we would expect the credit numbers to level off over the remaining months of this year."

The banking data also showed a rise of 568 million punts in Ireland's official external reserves to 5.722 billion, confirming that the central bank had been a net seller of the Irish pound in September to slow its advance against the mark, analysts said.
